say: Two of ours walked the east road to market and never arrived. No bodies, no carts, no word. It is the third time this month.
The flood road takes people and gives nothing back. Not even bones. Somebody is doing it neatly.
My cousin took the east road with a sack of dried fish. The sack came back. She didn't. Ask along the road who's taking walkers.
Walkers vanish where the road meets the flats. We can't spare men to watch it. You look like you could.
Somebody is picking that road clean of travellers. Ask the traders, ask the drifters.
accept: I will ask along the road.
I will find who it is.
accepted: Ask the Guild's wagon drivers, then the drifters who camp off the road. Somebody saw a lantern or a cart. Come back with a name.
Traders first, drifters second. Then the Anti-Slavers, if they will speak. The ones who sell people know the ones who steal them.
Follow the carts. Nobody takes that many without a buyer, and nobody buys without somebody talking.

say: The east road? Our wagons go in convoy now. Two drivers who passed alone said there was a man sat by the road, writing in a book.
Walkers, yes. We lose none because we don't walk. A driver told me of a man on a crate at the bend, writing, not looking up.
Don't take that road alone. A man sits by it with a ledger and he isn't waiting for a friend.
We pay for escorts. Walkers can't. Whoever it's knows that, and waits at the bend.
after: The drivers will not look at him. Ask the drifters who camp near there. They count the faces that pass.
I never saw him myself. Ask the drifters. They sleep closer to the road than any wagon would.
Nobody who stopped to talk to him is around to tell it. Try the drifters.
Ask the drifters. They sleep near the road and they count what passes.

say: We camp off the road now. Three nights ago a cart went by with no lantern and a man walking behind it, counting under his breath.
There was a line of walkers at dusk, nine or ten. In the morning the road was empty and the dust was all one way.
I'll tell you what I saw and no more. A man with a book, tapping the page twice for each one. Two taps, and they went into the cart.
We lost a boy that way. The Anti-Slavers keep a count of the taken. Ask them. I can't go near that road again.
after: Toward the flats, where the ground is soft. I did not follow. The Anti-Slavers did, once, and lost two.
Ask the ones who take in the runaways. They have a name for him.
The Anti-Slavers know his name. We only know his book.
The Anti-Slavers keep a tally of the taken. Ask them for a name.

say: We have a name for him. The Tallyman. Veldt Harrow. He sold to every market once. Now he sells to none.
Harrow. A slaver who stopped trading and started counting. We lost two of ours following his cart to the flats.
You're asking after the book. Good. Harrow keeps a ledger of the people he takes. We want it more than we want him.
Eleven walkers since the rains. That we know of. All Harrow's. Nobody is sold. Nobody is freed. Nobody is found.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: Ask the slavers. He was theirs once. They will not like it, but they know where his road runs.
The Slave Traders cut him loose. They are the only ones who will say where. Be careful how you ask.
He used to deal with the Traders. They will know the ground he works. We do not.
He was a slaver once. The slavers will tell you what he was and where he walks.

say: Harrow? He stopped selling to us two years ago. We don't know where the stock goes. He was good at the work, that's all I'll say.
Veldt Harrow works the floodwastes and the mud beyond. Where the ground is soft. I wouldn't ask what's under it.
He was a fair dealer once. Then the markets thinned and so did he. I hear he writes down every head he keeps. It's bad for business.
A man who won't sell is no use to us. Find him on the flood roads. Where the mud is deepest, there he is.
after: The flood roads, the mud country, wherever a cart can still be pulled. He moves. The book does not.
Four or five men with him, no more. He does not need more. The people go quietly.
I have told you where. Do not tell the Cities I was the one.
Go to the flood roads. Do not walk them at dusk. That is when the book comes out.

say: The Tallyman is dead? Then the road is only a road again. Take this. It's the village's thanks, and some of its savings.
No more walkers lost. You have done what the guards couldn't. Here's what we have gathered.
They found a book on him, you say? Then we know the names at last. Take the cats.
The east road is open and the fish will go to market. We owe you.
An Inquisitor rode north after a runaway from Rebirth. He did not write and he did not return. The Nation would know what ate him.
A servant of the Flame has vanished on the Nation's own roads. Don't tell me beasts. Beasts don't take the cloak.
The Inquisition won't speak his name, which means they're afraid. Find where he went. We'll say the prayers after.
He was a hard man to lose, brother. Somebody managed it. Start at the gates and ask who saw him leave.
A runaway, an Inquisitor, and a road that swallowed both. I want to hear what the road knows.
accepted: Begin at a gate. Guards log who goes out. Then the farmers on the northern fields, then a priest. Report when you know.
Ask the gate guards. Then the peasants who work the roads. They see everything and are believed by no one.
Gate first, farmers second, a priest third. Priests hear what no one else will say. Do not trust the ones who say nothing.
Find the track he took. Then find who he met. Bring me what you learn.

say: The Inquisitor? He rode out at dawn, alone. He said a runaway from Rebirth had friends on the road. We did not ask which friends.
I wrote him out myself. North road, one day's food. He promised to write back. He did not.
A grey cloak and a worse temper. He went through the north gate with his hood up and was not seen again. We were told not to ask.
The log says he left. The log doesn't say he came back. That's all a log is for.
after: Ask the farmers on the northern fields. They sell to anyone who walks that road.
The farms along the north road. If he stopped to eat, they saw him.
Pilgrims, farmers, deserters, all use that road. The farmers will remember a grey cloak.
I have said more than the log allows. The farmers know the rest.

say: A man in a grey cloak asked me for water and who had fed a runaway. I said no one. He didn't believe me and I think he was right.
I saw him at the edge of my field. He met a Sentinel there who was on no patrol. They spoke, and they went into the trees together.
I fed a thin girl in dyed robes. I was afraid. The Inquisitor didn't ask me. A Sentinel did, and I told him yes.
The cloak and the Sentinel went into the hills together. Only the Sentinel came out. I am not saying anything else, brother.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: I do not know his name. Ask a priest. A deserter's name is whispered in confession before it is spoken anywhere else.
North and east, toward the pilgrim stones. Ask the priests. They hear the guilty before the guards do.
I want nothing to do with it. Speak to a priest. They are used to hearing what they cannot repeat.
Ask a priest. Whatever walked into those trees, a priest has heard its name.

say: A Sentinel confessed to me once that he could no longer say the words. His name was Morrow. He asked what the Flame does with a man who sees too much.
You ask after the grey cloak. Morrow came to me before he left his post. I told him to be silent. That may have been my sin.
Hask Morrow. A good soldier, once. He walked away from the Fist with his armour and orders. A man with nothing to lose.
Don't quote me. The Sentinel is Morrow, and he robs pilgrims now. Whatever became of the cloak, he knows.
after: Okran's Pride, near the roads the pilgrims use. Ask a pilgrim who has been robbed. They count themselves lucky to be alive.
Ask the pilgrims. They know the road better than the Paladins do, and he has taken from every one of them.
I cannot say what he did. I can say what he is. Go to the pilgrim road and ask who has been stopped.
The pilgrims know what he looks like. Ask one. They will tell you, and then they will pray.

say: A Sentinel took my offering at the pilgrim stones. He wore a grey cloak over his plate and it was too long for him.
He didn't speak. He took what I carried and let me walk. The cloak smelt of smoke and something sweeter. I didn't look at his face.
Hask Morrow. The pilgrims all say it. He wears a grey cloak with a torn collar now. Nobody says whose it was.
I thought he was a Sentinel. He was a man in a dead man's coat. Don't go near the stones unless you carry no coin.
after: In Okran's Pride, where the pilgrim road runs. Take care. He prays while he robs.
Alone, I think. A man who has broken his oath does not keep company.
Go with the Flame, brother. I will not go back that way.
You will not need to look hard. He is the one who does not run from the Flame.

say: Morrow is dead? And the cloak? Then the Inquisitor won't be found, and the Nation will say he was lost. Take this for the truth.
A deserter in a dead man's coat. The Fist won't speak of it. The Flame is grateful. Here's the Nation's coin.
You followed the cloak to the end. The Inquisition thanks you quietly, which is the only way it thanks.
The pilgrim road is safe, brother. We'll say a prayer for the Inquisitor.
A convoy ended on the south shore. The drivers were found at the tide line and the cargo was gone. Someone took their time over it.
Six wagons, six drivers. We found the wagons. The drivers were staked below the tide mark. Who knows the tide that well?
Dead men and empty wagons on the sand. My cousin drove the third. I want to know who tied the knots.
A caravan doesn't die by accident. This one died slowly, on a beach. Walk the coast and ask what was heard.
The sea didn't do this. The knots were too neat. Find who ties traders to the shore.
accept: I will ask along the coast.
I will find who did it.
decline: The coast is not my business.
accepted: Ask the shore folk who found them. Then the Mercenary Guild, who sold the guards. Then the Guild clerks who filed the route.
Fishers first, mercenaries second, the Guild third. Someone sold the route and the hour. That is a short list.
Find who knew the road and the tide. Then find who took the cargo. The two are not always the same.
Walk the coast. Ask who saw wagons and who saw none. Come back with a name.

say: I found the wagons at first light. The tide had been in and out again. The drivers were staked on the flat, facing the sea.
I'll tell you what I saw and no more. Wagons, stakes, ropes tied by someone who knew the knots. Whoever it was knew the tide table better than I do.
They had been there a day. The water had risen twice and fallen twice. They were alive for the first rise.
Don't ask me for more. I cut the ropes and buried what the sea left. The Guild paid a little, and I took it, and I don't feel well about it.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: Two mercenaries went with them. Neither was on the sand. Ask the Mercenary Guild.
Hired guards, two of them. They were not among the dead. Ask the Guild who hired them out.
I saw no one. I saw the marks of boots and the marks of a keel. Ask the Mercenary Guild about the guards.
The Guild will say the route was secret. Ask them who filed it, then watch their faces.

say: We sold two guards to that convoy. Neither came back. The rate was cheap because the road was cheap.
Two of ours rode with the wagons. We found one boot. The Guild keeps contracts, and the contract says the route was filed with the Traders.
The convoy took the shore road because someone told them it was clear. Somebody wanted that road used on that day.
Our guards were good. Whoever took them did not fight them, I think. They were given up. That is how it looks.
after: The Traders Guild filed it. Ask them who handled the paper. They will not like the question.
Ask the Guild clerks. A route is only secret if the clerks keep it.
I have a guess and no proof. The Traders Guild keeps the proof. Ask there.
Ask the Traders Guild. A filed route is a spoken route.

say: The route was filed with us. Nobody leaked it. It didn't need leaking. Marta Cull knows which wagons pass at which tide.
A Reaver woman holds the southern shore. Marta Cull. They call her the Brine-Wife. She takes the cargo and the crew and she takes her time.
Nine Guild hands lost to her last month. The ninth was a clerk. We don't talk about it.
The Brine-Wife. Marta Cull. She ties salvagers to the tide line and counts the waves. We lost this convoy to a habit, not a plan.
after: Ask someone who walks the coast. The Red Coast, the Old Beach, the Old Pits. A drifter will know where her people sit.
We tried. We sent four. We sent the contract after them. Ask the drifters on the beaches. They live nearer to her than we do.
She has Reavers with her, enough to fill a boat. The drifters know the beach. Ask them.
Ask the drifters on the beaches. They live closer to her than a clerk ever will.

say: The Brine-Wife? We don't camp on the Old Beach. We've seen the stakes. Some are new.
She works the Red Coast and the Old Beach, wherever the tide leaves a salvager helpless. Her people are Reavers. They aren't kind to anyone.
I saw the wagons from the dunes. I saw the stakes. I didn't stay to see who came back for the cargo.
Marta Cull keeps to the south shore and the old pits behind it. You'll know the place by the stakes at the tide line.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: South, along the coast. Follow the stakes. When you see rope in the sand, you are near.
Reavers, a dozen. They do not sleep on watch. Come when the tide is out.
The Old Pits are behind her. Do not let the tide catch you there. She will not.
Do not wait for the tide. She does not. Take what you can carry and leave early.

say: The Brine-Wife is dead? Then the tide is only the tide again. Take this. It is what the convoy's families gave, and what the Free Traders added.
No more stakes at the tide line. My cousin won't know, but I do.
You ended the Brine-Wife. The south shore will be quiet for a month.
A convoy lost, a woman ended. It doesn't balance, but it's the best the coast offers.
There's a Skeleton that won't stop talking. It says a sum, a road and a count, over and over. Something was done to it.
One of ours repeats a sum of money. It does not know why. A Skeleton should not do that. Learn what was done to it.
The one by the wall hasn't stopped speaking since it was brought in. The loop holds a debt.
I've heard it speak four thousand times. A penny. A count. A hat. I'd like to know what it describes.
A damaged Skeleton talks without rest. The words are an account. Someone wrote the account. Find them.
accepted: It says a sum, then a road, then a count. Ask the traders who use roads, and a repairer who reads memory cells. Return when you know the speaker.
A sum, a road, a count. Ask who takes tolls on a road. Ask who can read a burned loop. Then ask who wears a hat.
Traders know the sum. Repairers know the loop. Ask them both. Then come back.

say: A penny a cart. That's the toll. Pay it and your cart goes through. Don't pay it and your cart is broken, and you with it. We pay. Everyone pays.
A Skeleton on the road with a book. It takes a penny and writes it down. The Guild finds it cheaper than the alternative.
It's a count of carts. Forty protected, six killed, he says. The Guild has stopped correcting him.
A sum, a road, a count. That's a toll booth with no booth. The Guild pays and doesn't talk about it.
after: A repairer would know the loop. Ask the Tech Hunters. They keep a bench for that kind of work.
I do not know the Skeleton's name. A repairer might read it. Ask the Tech Hunters.
Ask someone who can read a burned loop. The Tech Hunters have the tools.
The Tech Hunters keep benches for broken loops. Ask one who repairs.

say: A talking loop? That is a memory cell burned on repeat. Whoever did it wanted the thing to say what it had been told. A toll collector, perhaps.
I can tell you the voice was shaped for a ledger. Numbers first, then a name, then a threat. The name is missing.
Burned on purpose. A Skeleton doesn't do this to itself. Someone stripped its memory and left the sum behind.
The loop ends with a title and a hat. I cannot say whose. Ask the Skeletons.
after: A Skeleton town would know who is missing a collector. Ask the barman. They hear everything.
It cannot be mended without losing what it says. Ask the Skeletons who they lost.
Ask where a collector went missing. The Skeleton barmen keep that kind of count.
Ask the Skeletons who they are missing. They keep that count better than we do.

say: Tuppence. He took our collector three months ago and stripped his memory. The one you heard is what was left.
Mister Tuppence. He sells road protection. The one who talks was his collector. When he stopped being useful, he was left to loop.
Tuppence did it. The voice belonged to one of ours. A good one. He joined the toll because the toll paid. Then Tuppence did not need him.
A Skeleton with a ledger and a hat. Tuppence. We don't drink with him. He doesn't drink at all.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: The old pits and the robot graveyard. He charges a penny a cart. He keeps the rest.
He does not like loose ends. The talker was the last. Ask the Mercenary Guild about the toll booth. They have paid it.
Not alone. A handful of Skeleton bandits follow him. They are orderly. That is the worst of it.
The Mercenary Guild escorts convoys down that road. Ask who has paid the toll.

say: We escorted a convoy past the Robot Graveyard. There's a toll there. A Skeleton in a hat, a ledger, and six others who don't blink.
Tuppence. We paid. The Guild's policy is to pay a penny when a penny will do. It was a great deal more than a penny.
A fair-minded bandit. He counts every cart, every coin. If you haven't paid, he writes it down. If you don't pay, he writes you down.
The Robot Graveyard has a landlord. He wears a hat. He charges a toll. I advise you to carry a coin and not argue.
after: The Robot Graveyard, the old pits, the Blister Sands. He moves with the carts.
Six or seven. They do not need more. Their ledger is longer than your sword.
He did not say much. He wrote it all down. That is how I knew we were in trouble.
Carry a penny. If you must argue with him, argue after he has been paid.

say: Tuppence is closed? Then the talker will stop. Or it won't, but it will have an ending. Take this for the account.
The ledger is shut. The Skeleton by the wall is quiet. I do not know what that means, but the account is balanced. Here.
A toll collected in full. I'll log it.
You found who wrote the account and ended it. Skeletons rarely pay for justice.
Old machines walk in the Ashlands. Not wandering. Walking, in one direction. I'd like to know who's calling them.
A cut limb came in with a signal burned into its joint. It isn't a code I know. It points toward the domes. Who gathers machines?
Cat-Lon is exiled in the domes and has no army left. Yet machines gather there. Find what he wants with them.
Machines don't choose a direction. Someone chose it for them. Ask the repairers, the scavengers, the old ones.
A signal in the dead frame. A heading toward the Ashlands. I want to know what answers it.
accept: What does he want with them?
accepted: Tech Hunters see machines more than anyone. Ask them. Then the Hive, who built the limbs. Then the old Skeletons, who remember him.
Scavengers first. Then the Hive workshops. Then the old Skeletons. Come back when you know why they walk.
Ask who has seen them move. Ask who built them. Ask who remembers the one they follow.

say: Machines in the Ashlands? I have seen them. Not attacking, not fleeing. Walking in lines, every one facing the domes.
I followed a broken walker for half a day. It didn't stop for me. It didn't stop for the sand. It stopped at a wall and stood there.
They aren't scavenging. They're arriving. That's what makes the hair stand up. A machine that arrives is a machine that was told to.
I found a limb with a signal etched in the joint. The same heading as the rest. A call, not a command.
after: Ask someone who knows the old workshops. The Hive made the first limbs. They will know a signal when they see one.
I am a scavenger, not a builder. The Hive built the limbs. Ask them.
The workshop Hivers know old signals. I do not.
The Hive built the first limbs. A Hiver at a workshop will know the pattern.

say: The limbs are Hive work, long ago. Some machines still answer an old signal. The signal isn't ours. We don't know whose it is.
A call that old doesn't travel by itself. Someone repeats it. A tower, a machine, a mind.
The work was ours. The calling isn't. We don't use signals to move what we build. We ask it, and it goes.
The pattern is old. It answers to someone who spoke to machines when no one else would.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: Ask the old Skeletons. They remember who spoke so. I will not say the name.
The Skeletons in the Black Desert. They remember what the humans forgot.
Ask the ones who remember the Empire. They will tell you who called.
Ask a Skeleton from the Black Desert. They remember the Empire.

say: Cat-Lon and Tinfist worked well together once. Now one hides in a dome. A king with no subjects calls the only things left that obey.
Cat-Lon wanted to rebuild. He wanted to mend what the old world broke. He's alone now. A man alone builds an audience from scrap.
He ruled gently at first, they say, then not gently. The softness is gone. The grip is not. He gathers what he can still command.
You ask what Cat-Lon wants with machines. He wants anyone left to hear him. They are the only ones who do.
after: The domes in the Ashlands. A throne and a few who still answer. Ask the Machinists. They have the maps.
Ask Finch or Iyo, the Machinists. They keep track of what moves in the Ashlands.
He is where the machines go. Ask the Machinists to point.
The Machinists have the maps. Ask Finch or Iyo.

say: The signal has a source in the Ashlands. A dome, a throne. I have the readings.
Every machine in the survey moves toward the same point. Cat-Lon's Exile. He does not call them to fight. I think he calls them to be heard.
I can't prove it. A signal repeated across a thousand years, and a king who never stopped sending. The machines never stopped answering.
If you go, take more than a sword. He's the strongest of the Empire's remains, and nobody has asked him what he wants.
after: Whatever he wants, I do not think it is yours to give. Be careful.
He is. He was a ruler, he is a prisoner, and he is a machine. Pick which one you meet.
I do not think so. But you may be the first to ask.
Go if you must. The domes will not be quiet when you arrive.

say: Cat-Lon is silent. The machines have stopped walking. It took a thousand years to get here. The Black Desert will speak of this, quietly.
You ended a king. The signal is gone and the lines have scattered. Take the pay. It's little for what it meant.
The old Empire ends with a throne and a dead signal. I'll log it. Here's what we owe.
Mad Cat-Lon is dead. I don't know whether to mourn or to count the savings. Both.
I have followed Tinfist's raids for a year. They come wider and wilder. A man like that wants a loud ending. I mean to give him a quiet one. Do you?
Tinfist is the largest bounty on the continent. His raids have changed. Someone is feeding him routes, or he has stopped caring.
Every hunter who went for Tinfist alone is in the ground. I'd prefer a pair of eyes that isn't mine. Find where he rests between raids.
A Skeleton doesn't tire. But his raids are further apart and they hit harder. I think something is ending. Find what, before it ends without us.
Do not tell me he is a hero. Heroes do not leave caravans burning. Ask along his road.
accepted: Start with the Cities' scouts. They count patrols. Then the slavers he hits. Then the old Skeletons who knew him. Report to a hunter, any hunter.
Scouts first, slavers second, Skeletons third. Each knows a different piece. Put them together and you have where he sleeps.
Ask who he hits and who he misses. The misses are the map. Come back when you know where.
Learn his pattern. A man who strikes at dusk sleeps at dawn. Find where.

say: Our scouts count the Anti-Slaver patrols. They shrink. Tinfist's raids don't. He's spending fighters like water.
Tinfist moves in a ring around the slaver roads, and every ring he draws is smaller. He's closing in on somewhere. Or something is closing in on him.
Scout reports say he's thinner on the ground. Fewer ninjas, more rage. A leader who spends his own is a leader with a deadline.
I have counted his raids for two months. They bunch. When a man bunches his raids he is preparing to stop.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: Ask the slavers who bear the raids. They know which roads he skips. Those roads are where he sleeps.
The Slave Traders feel every raid. Ask them which roads he does not touch.
Ask the slavers. The roads he leaves alone are the ones he lives beside.
The slavers feel every raid. Ask them where he does not strike.

say: He hits at dusk, never at night. He knows our routes better than we do. Someone gives him the roads, or he has watched them for years.
There's a stretch he never touches. A day's walk, no more. Every other road, he has burned.
Tinfist spares the slaves and burns the wagons. He doesn't rest near the roads he raids. He comes from somewhere with water and a wall.
Do you know what's worse than losing a wagon to Tinfist? Losing it to him in the same place twice. He doesn't repeat unless he's tired.
after: Ask the old Skeletons in the Black Desert. They knew him before he was a terror.
A Black Desert Skeleton knows what he fears. I do not. Ask there.
The Black Desert Skeletons remember what he was. You will want that.
A Skeleton from the Black Desert knew him before he was a terror. Ask one.

say: Tinfist and Cat-Lon made a good pair once. Now Tinfist fights for the humans and Cat-Lon is lost. The one who stayed is the one wearing thin.
He was a student of Gatwood the Soft, who never took a life. Tinfist has taken many. The gap is the thing that wears him thin.
A Skeleton can't grow old. But he can grow tired of what he does. Tinfist is wearing thin. He won't say. He will fight until he drops.
Why do you want him? Because someone will, soon. Better a hand that knows what he was than a hand that doesn't.
after: He sleeps in the Anti-Slavers' own city. Grey sits at his side. Ask a Traders Guild man. They know where the raids start.
The Anti-Slavers' city is where he rests. It is not a place that welcomes a hunter.
He goes home between raids. Ask the Guild wagoners. They watch from the edge.
The Guild's wagoners watch the edges of his ground. Ask them.

say: The Anti-Slavers keep a city, and he rests there. The raids start from that edge. Nobody goes near it by choice.
Our wagoners say the patrols thin out near his city. He's there when he isn't out. You'll find him between raids.
I won't tell you how to find him. I'll tell you the raids start from the south and west. You can work out the rest.
A convoy that came near was turned back by a Skeleton with bare fists. The wagoners say he didn't even run.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: Grey will be there, and the ninjas. Do not go alone. Do not go slowly.
Bring your best. He was a student of someone who never took a life, and he has made up for it.
He will not run. He never does. That is how you will know it is him.
He does not hide. That is his advantage. Go with more than one blade.

say: Tinfist is dead? The largest bounty on the continent, and a quiet hunter ended it. The Cities will pay a fortune. Here is mine.
A Skeleton doesn't tire, I said. I was wrong. You've done what no one else could.
He fought to the last, I hear. That's the pity of it. The raids will stop. The world won't be better.
I didn't think a stranger could do it. The slavers will celebrate. I'll drink. Take your pay.

states: Head of Agriculture killed by player
say: I study the old failures. The domes failed in an order: the harvest, the police, the cult. I want the first failure told by someone who was there.
The Head of Agriculture still keeps his ledger in the first dome. He is the only witness left. A dead witness is only a body.
Rhinobot helped with anything. Hat-12 enforced anything. The Head of Agriculture reported. Someone must read the reports. Find the one who wrote them.
Skeletons forget by choice. I'd rather remember. The Ashlands domes hold a clerk who knows how the Empire began to fail.
I have records, but no voice. A voice would be the Head of Agriculture's. I need him whole, in a cage if necessary. I won't have him killed.
accepted: Ask the Tech Hunters who have walked the domes. Ask the Machinists, who keep the old records. Then the Skeletons who remember. Bring him alive.
Scavengers see the ruins. Machinists read the records. Old Skeletons remember. Start there. The cage is the last step.
Go to those who have walked the Ashlands. Learn the order of the failure. Then bring the clerk out.
A witness is worth more than a ruin. Learn where he sits. Return when he is in custody.

say: The first dome? A thin old official sits in a room full of thralls and keeps writing in a ledger. I didn't go further. He didn't look up.
Thralls guard fields that aren't there. They guard a man who counts what isn't grown. I counted three of them for each stalk of nothing.
I found a dome with the doors open. Inside, a clerk and an Empire's worth of grain stores, all empty. He told me the harvest was late.
A record room, half collapsed, and a man sitting in it. He called me by a name that wasn't mine. He asked for the requisitions.
after: The Machinists read the old Empire records. Ask Finch or Iyo. They would want to know a clerk still lives.
The Machinists keep the Empire's paper. Ask them what the harvest numbers said.
Ask Finch or Iyo. They will know whether the records agree with what I saw.
Ask the Machinists. Finch or Iyo will tell you what the records say.

say: The Empire's records say the harvest failed first. Before the police moved on any cult. That's the order nobody tells.
The weekly reports from the Head of Agriculture are in the archive. Every week he wrote the same sentence.
A crop failure becomes a shortage. A shortage becomes a riot. A riot becomes a crackdown. Hat-12 was last, not first.
The first dome is where it began. The Head of Agriculture couldn't have foreseen the rest.
after: Ask the old Skeletons what they remember of the thralls. They guarded what the Empire valued.
Skeletons who lived through it remember the guards. They will tell you what else the clerk guarded.
The Skeletons in the old towns remember. Ask a barman. They overhear.
Ask a Skeleton from the Black Desert. They remember the guards.

say: Rhinobot wanted to help. He had no way to judge. Hat-12 wanted order. He had no way to stop. The clerk wrote reports. No one read them.
The Head of Agriculture carried the first sheaf at a festival, so I hear. Skeletons and humans, side by side. Then the harvest failed.
If you want the story told, take the clerk alive. A dead clerk cannot read his own ledger. The thralls do not hear him now.
I remember the festival. I do not remember the harvest. That is how the Empire died, a fact at a time.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: The first dome in the Ashlands. A cage will serve. He will not resist. He has forgotten how.
Take him quietly. The thralls will not understand. He does.
He will ask whether you have a requisition. Say yes. It will be easier.
A free trader walked that edge once. Ask one who has seen the wall.

say: I carried scrap to the edge of the Ashlands once. A thrall stood at the wall and didn't move. Behind him a man was counting.
Don't go in with a sword. The thralls guard a ledger. If you disturb the ledger the clerk won't speak.
A cage and a cart. That's how I'd do it. A clerk who hasn't left a room in a thousand years is no fighter.
People pay to see a thing like that in a cage. I wouldn't. I'd just want to hear what he wrote.
after: Be gentle. He is a witness. He is not an enemy. The thralls will make a fuss, though.
Watch the thralls. They do not forget their posts even when the post is gone.
If you take him, take the ledger too. The words are the point.
Go gently. The dome has enough ghosts without you adding a witness.

report.state: Head of Agriculture imprisoned by player
say: The Head of Agriculture is in custody? Then the record can begin. Alive. That's more than I hoped.
A witness, caged and breathing. Skeletons seldom feel gratitude. I feel something close.
You brought out the clerk. The first dome has no one left to guard. The Empire's first failure will be written down. Take the cats.
I'll put every question to him, slowly. He won't mind. He has had a very long time to prepare. Here's your pay.
The Fogmen take the living, not the dead. That is not hunger. That is habit. Someone should ask why before the next one is carried off.
Three of ours went into the fog last month, carried, not dragged. Fogmen don't carry what they mean to waste.
I have stood a thousand watches. I've never seen a Fogman kill what it could carry. Find where they carry it, and to whom.
A Fog Prince eats the prisoners, I hear. The others sit round and watch. Someone taught them to wait.
Don't tell me they're beasts. Beasts don't hold a feast. Learn what the fog wants and put an end to the one who wants it.
accepted: Ask the town. Ask the Fishers, who sail near the isles. Ask the Hive, who know what the Fogmen were. Then find the one at the heart.
Mongrel first, then the Fishers, then the Hive. Put the pieces together. Then find what sits at the middle.
Anyone who has seen the poles can tell you more than I can. Listen. Then take it to the Prince.
Begin with whoever lost someone. They will talk. Then end it where it starts.

say: My sister's boy went to the shore at night and did not come back. They found his boots. Only boots. They carry people. They do not drop them.
I heard screaming from the fog last night. The same voice all night, then none. I didn't sleep. I don't want to guess what that meant.
The Fogmen come at the walls when they're many. When they're few, they take the stray. The strays don't come back.
I know three people the fog took. I knew them well. I can't remember their faces any more, and I think that's a mercy.
after: The Fishers sail close to the isles. Ask them what stands on the shore.
Ask the Fishers. They have seen the poles.
A Fisher will tell you what the Fogmen build. I will not.
Ask a Fisher. They see the shore from the water, and the water does not lie.

say: We don't fish the north shore. Tall poles stand there. Some are bare. Some aren't. The Fogmen sit round them and make a noise.
I saw a Deathyard once, from the water. Poles, stakes, bones tied together. Some Fogmen sang and some ate.
Prisoners are tied to the poles. Some are fed to the Princes. Some are worshipped. They don't seem to see a difference.
I'll tell you what the fog is. It's a place where the dead aren't dead and the living aren't living. That's all I know.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: The Hive know what the Fogmen were. They will not like being asked. Ask a worker.
Ask a Hiver. Fogmen are their cousins. They will have something to say.
A Hive worker would know the sickness. I only know the poles.
The Hive know what the sickness was. Ask a worker.

say: The Fogmen are cousins. A parasite took their minds and drives them from within. Nothing can be done for them now.
They were workers once. When the sickness took the Deadhive, the drones turned. They don't remember.
The Fog Princes are the sickness at its fullest. Where one sits, the others gather. They're the voice the rest obey.
Don't ask us to mourn them. We did, once. It didn't help. Ask the one who won't stop the fog.
after: Seek a Prince. A Prince is the heart of the pack. Break it and the rest fray.
The Princes sit near the poles. There is a tower on the islands where one waits. You will not need a map.
A Prince leads them. A Prince can be ended. That is all the Hive can offer.
A Hiver merchant will tell you where the Prince sits. They sell more than goods.

say: I've heard what you ask. The Fog Prince sits in the Tower of Fog, in the dark, with a feast of poles around him.
The Princes hold the fog. Where one dies, the others mourn. For a month, the fog is quiet. Then another sits in the empty place.
We sell what you need. We don't go to the isles. Don't tell the Hive I said it, but the Prince is only the sickness with a crown.
You carry a question the Hive has asked for a long time. If you finish the Prince, tell us.
after: The Tower of Fog on its island off the west coast. The Deadhive Overrun to the north. Wherever the fog is thickest.
Take armour. The Fogmen will carry anyone they can lift.
Do not fall. They will not kill you. That is the worst part.
Do not go to the isles at night. The fog is thickest then, and so are they.

say: The Prince is dead? The fog is a little thinner. They will not carry any more of ours, for a while. Take this. Mongrel remembers.
You ended the one at the middle. The Fogmen will find another. But it takes them a month. A month is a great deal.
No more screaming from the fog, for now. I slept last night.
You have done what the watch could not. I will tell the town. Take the cats, and do not go near the fog again.
My sister was in Rebirth. She got out. A woman in dyed robes does not go unseen. I heard she went toward the ash.
They put her in dyed robes and called her renewed. She walked out the night after. Nobody has seen her since.
The Nation doesn't lose anyone, people say. Rebirth never loses a soul. I want to know what became of her.
She ran from the Nation with nothing but a robe. I can't go back north. Ask along the road.
I do not want revenge. I want to know. Ask who saw a woman in dyed robes on the road to the ash.
accept: I will ask along the road.
accepted: Ask the Anti-Slavers who take in the runaways. Then the road folk. Then the scavengers at the edge of the ash. Someone saw a robe.
Anti-Slavers first, drifters second, scavengers third. Then the Nation's own Paladins, who will know what lives in the ash.
A robe is not a face, but it is something. Ask who saw it. Come back with what you learn.
I will wait here. I cannot go further. Ask the ones who help the runaways.

say: A woman in a dyed robe? We took in nineteen last year. One didn't stay. She said she would rather freeze than be a guest.
We keep no records. Records are for the Nation. But I remember a runaway in dyed robes who would not take our bread. She asked where the ash was.
Rebirth leaves marks. Some people carry them for life. The one you describe asked about the ash. We told her not to go.
We offered her a place. She walked into the ash instead. It was her choice, and it was a bad one.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: Ask the drifters who camp along the edge. They watch who goes in.
The drifters on the road to the ash will have seen her. Ask them.
Someone watched her go. Ask the ones who live at the edge.
The drifters along the road to the ash will have seen her. Ask them.

say: I saw someone in a grey robe at the edge of the ash. She didn't look back.
A woman, alone, at dusk. She didn't carry food or water. I thought she was a ghost until she asked for the road.
She was running, I think. Not from anything we saw. From something she carried with her.
We offered her water. She drank and walked on. In the morning the dust was one way, into the ash.
after: Tech Hunters work the ash edge. They go in and out. Ask them what they found.
A scavenger might have found where she stopped. Ask the Tech Hunters.
Ask the ones who dig in the ruins. They find what the ash leaves.
The Tech Hunters work the ash edge. Ask them what the dust gave up.

say: A dyed robe, pinned to a post at the ash edge, fresh. As if someone wanted it found. The ground around it was scuffed, then clean.
I saw a man in a coat that wasn't cloth. He was folding something small and soft, very carefully.
We keep to the ruins. The edge of the ash belongs to a thing in a coat of skins. We were told to leave the robe where it hung.
I found a robe nailed to a post. It was not rotten. Whoever placed it came back to see if anyone would take it.
after: The Holy Nation knows the thing in the coat. They will not tell scavengers. Ask a Paladin.
Ask a Paladin. The Nation has a name for what lives there.
I do not know the name. The Holy Nation does. They keep a list.
A Holy Nation Paladin will know what walks the edge of the ash. Ask one.

say: We know the Tailor. His name is Peel. He works the ash edge near Skinner's Roam. If your runaway took that road, you will find only her robe.
Aldous Peel. A skinner, a thing in a coat of faces. The Nation has marked him for burning. He does not come to the roads. The roads go to him.
A runaway from Rebirth in dyed robes who went into the ash? She didn't walk out. Peel doesn't let go of what he finds.
The Tailor is not on the Nation's list because he is hard to catch. He is on it because he is a sin. Whoever sends you has my pity.
reply: Where should I go from here?
after: Burn the coat. The Nation will pay for it. Do not look at what is sewn into the lining.
He works the ashlands and the Roam. Go with the Flame, and take more than one blade.
She was not the first. She will not be the last unless someone ends him.
Go to the ash edge. Take more than a blade. Do not read what is sewn in the coat.

say: Peel is dead? Then she isn't in the ash anymore. She's only in the ground. I thank you. I didn't want her alive, only found.
The Tailor is ended. I'll tell her name to the dust. Take the cats. It's what I saved.
You found where she stopped. That's more than the Nation gave me.
I won't ask what you saw. I'll ask only that you don't tell me. Take the cats.
Walkers go missing on the east road. Not caravans, walkers. Somebody who knows how few of us there are.
Two went to market and never got there. Nobody found a bone.
I don't take the road alone anymore. Neither does anyone who has counted the empty beds.
A road that eats people and leaves the wagons. It's quieter than bandits and worse.
The east road has a toll nobody pays in cats. Drivers speak of a man at the bend, writing.
Our drivers carry spare rope and a second lantern. They say it's for the road. It isn't for the road.
Someone on the flood road keeps a book of faces. I'd rather be a stranger to him.
The Guild is losing walkers it never hired. That's a rare kind of theft.
They say a cart with no lantern goes east after dusk. The ones who watch it don't sleep well.
Two taps on the page and they go in the cart. That's what a drifter told me. I told him to stop talking.
I hear the Anti-Slavers followed a cart to the flats and lost two. They haven't tried again.
Whoever it's has a name now. The Tallyman. People say it like a prayer they don't trust.
Veldt Harrow sold to anyone once. He stopped. Nobody knows where the stock goes, and that bothers me more than the selling.
A slaver who buries his goods. Some men can't stand a shrinking market.
The Tallyman keeps count to the head. A man like that's frightening because he's orderly.
He moves between the flood roads and the mud. Where the ground is soft.
The Tallyman is dead. Somebody found the book and the names. The east road breathes again.
Veldt Harrow is gone. They say his ledger went into the mud with him, then somebody dug it out.
No more walkers lost on the east road. I'll believe it in a month.
They buried the Tallyman in his own soft ground. The fishers say it was a courtesy he didn't give.
An Inquisitor went north and didn't come back. The Fist says he's on a long errand. The Fist says many things.
A grey cloak left by the north gate and nobody saw it return. We are told not to talk of it.
The Inquisition has gone quiet. Quiet means a man is missing and nobody wants his name said.
A runaway from Rebirth and an Inquisitor on her heels. Neither came back. Make of that what you will.
The Holy Nation lost one of its hounds on the north road. They're very quiet about it.
An Inquisitor missing and a Rebirth girl gone. The Nation's roads aren't as safe as its priests say.
I heard a Holy man in grey went north to fetch a runaway. Neither is on any road I've walked.
If the Nation can't keep its own Inquisitors, why do they preach about keeping us?
The farmers on the north road say a Sentinel was seen speaking with a grey cloak. They went into the trees together.
A Sentinel off his patrol. Everyone knows his face and no one will say his name.
I heard a farmer fed a runaway and hasn't slept since. Someone should tell him the girl isn't the danger.
A priest told me a Sentinel asked what the Flame does with a man who sees too much. I didn't ask what the answer was.
Hask Morrow has a new cloak. Grey, torn at the collar. Nobody asks where it came from.
The pilgrim stones aren't safe. A Sentinel in someone else's coat takes the offerings now.
Morrow wears a cloak that is too long for him. The pilgrims say it is a kindness not to look.
If you meet a Sentinel at the stones, don't argue. He prays while he takes your purse.
The grey cloak is found, I heard. Nobody will say where. The Inquisition has stopped asking.
Morrow is dead and the Nation has stopped saying his name. The runaway is gone from the records too.
A Sentinel fell in Okran's Pride. The Inquisitor is a ghost in a ledger. The Nation closes the pages quickly.
I heard the Inquisitor was never found. They say it very softly.
A convoy died on the south shore. They found the drivers at the tide line.
Six wagons and no one to drive them. The tide knew more than the guards did.
I won't take the shore road this month. The Guild says it's safe. The Guild didn't see the stakes.
The crows were at the wagons before the Guild was. That tells you everything about how fast news travels.
Two mercenaries went with that convoy and nobody has seen them since. The Guild isn't saying much.
A caravan that dies on the sand is a bad advertisement for the road.
They say the knots were too neat for bandits. Bandits tie quickly, and they don't stay to watch the water.
I heard somebody sold the route. I hope whoever it was was paid well.
The Mercenary Guild says the route was filed with the Traders. The Traders say everyone knows the tide table.
A fisher cut the ropes and buried what the sea left. He doesn't go near the flats anymore.
Nobody talks about the stakes. Everybody has seen them. That's how you know it isn't an accident.
A Reaver was seen near the old pits wearing a driver's boots. It's what I heard.
The Brine-Wife. That's a name the Guild says very quietly now.
Marta Cull holds the south shore. They say she times the water with her fingers.
Stakes at the tide line, new ones. If you see rope in the sand, you're too close.
Nine Guild hands lost to one woman. The Guild would rather you didn't count.
The Brine-Wife is dead. The south shore has gone quiet. The stakes are still there.
Marta Cull fell on her own beach. The tide came in and took what it took.
Whoever ended the Brine-Wife did the coast a favour. Whoever filed the route should still be asked questions.
The shore road is open again. I will use it in the spring.
A Skeleton sits in the town and won't stop speaking. A sum, a road, a count. Nobody can make it stop.
I hear a Skeleton is talking itself to scrap. It says a number and a hat. I did not ask what it meant.
The talking one has been at it for a month. The others pretend not to hear. That's Skeleton politeness.
Somebody burned a loop into a Skeleton and left it to run. It's the most horrible thing I've heard in a long time.
A penny a cart on the robot roads. Pay it. Don't argue. Don't look at the hat.
There's a Skeleton on the Robot Graveyard road who charges tolls. The Guild pays. The Guild doesn't say how much.
A Skeleton with a ledger, collecting. It sounds orderly until you try not to pay.
Forty carts protected, six killed. That's the arithmetic of a Skeleton who enjoys his work.
A memory cell burned on repeat. That's no accident. Someone left a toll collector's voice to loop.
The loop ends in a hat. The name is scraped. I've seen the work. It was careful.
Skeletons don't forget their own. They know who's missing a collector. They don't say.
A repairer told me the voice was shaped for a ledger. The ledger is still out there.
Mister Tuppence. A Skeleton in a hat, with a book and six who don't blink. Don't carry less than a penny.
Tuppence took a collector and left his voice. A bandit who recycles. I can't decide what's worse.
The Robot Graveyard has a landlord. He wears a hat. The talker is his leftover.
He writes down every cart that doesn't pay. And then, if he feels like it, he writes down the carters.
Mister Tuppence is closed. The ledger was found and burned. The talker has stopped, people say. Or it has gone quiet.
The toll on the Robot Graveyard road is no more. Nobody believes it yet. I'll pay a penny anyway, out of habit.
A Skeleton in a hat is dead. The road is a little less orderly now. I find I miss the order.
Tuppence fell with his ledger. They say the numbers kept adding after he was gone.
Old machines are walking in the Ashlands. In lines. All the same way. Don't stand in their path.
A broken walker followed me for half a day and stopped at a wall. It didn't look at me. It didn't need to.
Machines don't move for no reason. Somebody is calling them. I don't like it.
I found a limb with a signal etched in the joint. I put it back. I didn't touch the next one.
Machines in the ashes, people say. Walking to a dome. I'll keep to the roads.
A mad king in a dome calls the dead machines. That's what the Skeletons say. I thought it was a story.
I don't go near the Ashlands. A man can lose his mind there, or something can take it.
The Tech Hunters are bringing back stories of machines that march. I pay for stories. I don't pay for those.
The Hive made the limbs. The calling is older. Nobody asks who built the first signal.
A signal like that isn't for killing. A signal like that's for gathering. Gathering for what?
The workshops say the pattern is Empire. The old Empire, the one before the Holy Nation had a name for itself.
A machine doesn't answer a call unless it was made to. Someone made them to, long ago.
Cat-Lon wants an audience. Machines were the last who would listen. That's what a Skeleton told me over a drink.
The king in the dome calls them. Nobody asks him why. Nobody who goes there asks anything.
Finch says the signal is a call to be heard. I think that is the saddest thing I have ever read.
He ruled a thousand years. He built civilisation and watched it fall. Now he builds a crowd from scrap.
The machines in the Ashlands have stopped. They stand where they were. I don't know if that's better.
Mad Cat-Lon is gone. The Skeletons won't talk about it.
The signal fell silent last week. A Tech Hunter said it was like a house with the last light put out.
An old king is dead and the machines don't know. They're still facing the dome.
Tinfist struck another wagon train. Dusk, as always. He leaves the slaves and burns the wagons.
The raids are wilder. I do not like it. A man who is losing hits harder before he falls.
He's fewer than he was. His ninjas thin out. Still he comes. That's the worst kind of enemy.
Somebody should end Tinfist before he ends the roads.
Tinfist isn't what he was. We don't say it where he can hear.
He fights like a man who has nowhere to be. That's how I know he isn't afraid.
I heard a Skeleton can hold on a thousand years. I heard Tinfist isn't planning to.
The hunters circle. He knows. He doesn't change his road. That's what bothers us.
A scout told me Tinfist's raids bunch. When a man bunches his raids, he's preparing to stop.
The roads he leaves alone are the ones he lives beside. A hunter's map is mostly gaps.
I counted the patrols. Fewer each month. Tinfist is spending what he has.
A quiet hunter is asking where he sleeps. Most hunters don't ask.
Tinfist and Cat-Lon. One of them is lost, and one is dying. I do not know which is worse.
He was a student of a man who never took a life. He has taken more than anyone.
A Skeleton can't grow old. But he can grow tired. I saw it in Tinfist's stance, long ago.
The Anti-Slavers' city is where he rests. It's a hard door to knock on.
Tinfist is dead. I don't know whether to cheer or sit down. A great many people won't sleep tonight.
The raids have stopped. The roads are quiet. The Anti-Slavers are very still.
A Skeleton hero is finished. The slave roads will be busy by spring.
They say he didn't run. They say he never did.
The domes in the Ashlands fell in an order. First the harvest, then the police, then the cult. Everyone tells it differently.
A clerk still keeps his ledger in the first dome. Nobody goes near him. They say he writes the same line every night.
The Empire didn't fall to an army. It fell to a thin harvest and the people who tried to fix it.
I've walked the dome road. The thralls don't move. They have forgotten what they're guarding.

states: Head of Agriculture imprisoned by player

say: The Ashlands have ruins with doors that open. I wouldn't go through them.
A scavenger came back from the domes and wouldn't talk. He sold his boots and left.
They say there is an old man in a dome who thinks the harvest is late. I do not know whether to laugh.
The Ashlands remember things the Nation would rather not. That's the safest thing I can say.

states: Head of Agriculture imprisoned by player

say: Rhinobot wanted to help. Hat-12 wanted order. The Head of Agriculture only wanted to be told he wasn't to blame.
Every week the clerk wrote the same sentence, and every week the Empire did not answer.
The Machinists have the reports. The order is harvest, shortage, riot, crackdown. Nobody tells it that way because it makes everyone guilty.
A historian told me he wants the clerk alive. I said that was a great deal to ask of a ruin.

states: Head of Agriculture imprisoned by player

say: A cage and a cart. That's how you take a clerk out of a dome. I'd pay to see it. I wouldn't pay to do it.
The thralls guard fields that aren't there. They guard a man who counts what isn't grown.
If you take the ledger, take it whole. The words are the point. The clerk is only the hand.
I don't like a world where a thousand-year-old clerk is the last honest witness. But it's the world.

states: Head of Agriculture imprisoned by player

say: They took the Head of Agriculture out of the first dome alive. The thralls stand where they stood, guarding nothing.
A clerk is in a cage, and a Skeleton is asking him questions. I wonder who finds the answers easier.
The Empire's first failure is being written down. At last. I don't know whether anyone will read it.
The first dome is silent. The ledger is gone. Someone said the clerk asked for a requisition. I didn't ask what that meant.

states: Head of Agriculture imprisoned by player

say: The Fogmen carry the living. That's the horror of it. They could drop them.
I heard screaming from the fog last night. The same voice, then none.
Three of ours went into the fog last month. Their boots washed up.
A Fogman that kills is a beast. A Fogman that carries is something else.
The fog islands are a bad place. They say the poles stand tall there and the Fogmen feast around them.
A man who sails near the isles hears things. He doesn't tell anyone.
I don't go north of Mongrel. The Fogmen are only half the reason.
A friend of mine went north to see the fog for himself. He saw it. That's all I can say.
The Fogmen are cousins. We don't speak of it. A parasite sits in their heads and drives them.
When a queen dies, some drones turn. That's the sickness. That's what the fog is.
A Fog Prince is the sickness at its fullest. Where he sits, the others gather.
The Hive remembers the Deadhive. It remembers it in the way you remember a tooth that's gone.
The Prince is in a tower on the isles, they say. Break him and the pack frays.
A Deathyard is poles and bones. Some sing, some eat. The Prince sits in the middle and doesn't eat at all.
The Hive won't go. The Mongrel watch won't go. Someone has to.
I heard a stranger is asking after the Prince. Nobody asks that and stays long in Mongrel.
A Fog Prince is dead. The fog is quiet.
The screaming stopped. The Fogmen sit on the shore in the evenings and do nothing. It's worse.
I heard another Prince will sit in the empty place within the month. I'll keep my boots on.
Whoever ended the Prince has my thanks. I won't meet them. I don't want to know what they saw.
A runaway from Rebirth walked into the ash in dyed robes. I don't think she walked out.
Rebirth never loses a soul, people say. They lose one every month. They don't say that part.
A woman in a dyed robe asked which way the ash was. We told her.
The Nation doesn't hunt its runaways in the ash. It leaves them to the ash.
Rebirth is a school, people say. Schools don't lose their students at night.
A girl ran from the Rebirth school and nobody gave chase. That's how I know the Nation is worried.
I heard a robe hangs on a post at the ash edge. The Nation doesn't take it down.
The ash takes runaways. I don't know whether the Nation approves. I know it doesn't stop it.
A dyed robe pinned to a post. Not rotten. Somebody put it there to be found.
The ash edge isn't a place for a woman alone. A man in a coat of skins walks there. I won't say more.
A scavenger told me he saw a man folding something small and soft.
We told the runaway to stay. She didn't. I think of it every night.
The Tailor works the ash edge and the Roam. He takes the living and wears the work.
Aldous Peel. The Nation marks him for burning and sends no one to burn him.
A coat of skins, a coat of faces. The runaways don't come back from that road.
The Holy Nation keeps a list of sins. The Tailor's name is at the top. Nobody has been sent to cross it out.
The Tailor is dead. The ash edge is quiet. A robe still hangs there.
Aldous Peel is no more. The runaways say it, very softly, as though the ash could hear.
They burned the coat. I'm told it took an hour. I'm told nobody stood close.
Somebody found out what became of the girl in the dyed robe. I don't want to know. I'm glad someone does.
